summary:
Risaralda falls squarely within Colombia's national legal framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on self-recognition without a surgical requirement, marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025. At least 41 trans women were killed nationally in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, and 13 in the first quarter of 2025 alone. Of 155 criminal investigations into LGBTQ killings, only three reached a verdict in the period reported, roughly 2 per cent, against an overall homicide-conviction rate of about 9 per cent.

Where armed groups operate, the risk is organised rather than incidental. In Caquetá department, armed groups circulated "social cleansing" flyers on the street and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign still running despite the 2016 peace agreement. Three armed men gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; she fled at night after hiding for a week. Trans women in Caquetá reported few options beyond hairdressing or sex work, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. In Guajira department, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Targeted killings also occur in ordinary urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, in April 2025; a 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands flailing in a creek unable to swim before she drowned, and she died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon. No one was arrested although police interrogated local residents. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, solidarity events were held in several cities, and her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was".

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

No source isolates Risaralda from this national pattern, so the national figures and the armed-group threat profile are what a visitor to the department should expect to face.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's statutory position is well ahead of most of its neighbours: marker change by notary since 2015, constitutional protection of self-recognition since 1993, marriage since 2016, and explicit trans and non-binary document markers since November 2025. The divergence between that statutory position and the homicide and conviction data is the defining feature of the country's profile.

The violence is not confined to remote conflict zones. The Millerey killing in Bello, in the Medellín metropolitan area, and the earlier fatal attacks recalled in reporting, including a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping and people killed in their homes and in a hairdresser, show that urban residence does not remove the risk. Gay men have also been lured through an application and killed.

Discrimination shapes economic exposure as much as physical safety. Reporting from Caquetá found that discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, which concentrates them in contact with the armed groups running the cleansing campaigns and increases exposure to threats and displacement; Tatiana Cespedes was forced to relocate twice.

International scrutiny is active and current. Graeme Reid's May 2025 mission, the UN Human Rights Committee's registered concern, and the July 2023 gender-persecution indictment by the Special Jurisdiction for Peace all sit alongside rising killing figures rather than displacing them.
localsOnly:
Colombian citizens change the sex marker on cédula and other government identification by signing a document before a notary, a route available since June 2015 and not dependent on surgery, judicial order, or psychiatric assessment. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 grounds recognition in self-recognition.

Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, which affects how residents are read by officials at banks, clinics, and police checkpoints.

Trans detainees have judicially protected rights within the prison system following a court ruling on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty.

A comprehensive trans law was still before the legislature in 2025, so residents continue to rely on the notary route, constitutional jurisprudence, and scattered court orders rather than a single statute covering housing, health, and employment.

Employment discrimination remains the ordinary condition outside major cities, with trans women reported as channeled mainly into hairdressing and sex work.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory contains a Risaralda-specific legal, enforcement, or incident finding. Whether armed-group cleansing campaigns or named kill lists have circulated in Risaralda, and whether the department has its own anti-discrimination ordinance or trans-specific protection programme, is unresolved and not sourced here.

The three-verdicts-from-155-investigations figure and the 9 per cent overall homicide-conviction comparison are reported without a stated reporting period in the inventory; the period against which they should be read is unresolved.

Whether the comprehensive trans law under consideration in 2025 has since been enacted is unresolved on this inventory.

The inventory does not establish whether the Attorney General's 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025 include the 13 trans people counted in the first quarter of the same year, so the two figures should not be added together.
